core_classification.analysis: Mr. Brooke directly avows that he loves Meg. The utterance primarily presents his loving state as true. Its courtship setting gives it slight undertaking force because it helps initiate a possible future engagement, but the words themselves do not clearly constitute a promise or commitment. Tender and emotionally charged delivery does not provide independent evidence of expressive/reflexive discharge.
core_classification.ambiguity: There is limited T/P ambiguity: the declaration is part of a marriage-oriented courtship exchange, but its core force remains an avowal rather than a definite relational undertaking.

utterance_status.description: Mr. Brooke directly addresses Meg and says, “I love you so much, dear,” while asking whether she cares for him.

contextual_interpretation: The declaration occurs during a deliberate courtship conversation. Brooke seeks reciprocal affection and later offers to wait while Meg learns whether she can love him, framing the avowal as persuasive and future-oriented. Meg is emotionally affected and ambivalent, while the narrator later notes Brooke’s confidence in his success. These features qualify the interaction but do not displace the utterance’s dominant truth-conditional force or establish reflex-like expression.

evidence.quotation_or_description: “I only want to know if you care for me a little, Meg. I love you so much, dear,”
evidence.supports: The explicit first-person declaration strongly supports truth-conditional avowal and places it within a request for reciprocal affection.

evidence.quotation_or_description: The narrator says Mr. Brooke added the declaration “tenderly.”
evidence.supports: This establishes affectionate delivery but, without evidence of blurting or affective loss of control, does not independently support expressive/reflexive force.

evidence.quotation_or_description: Brooke subsequently asks, “Will you try and find out?” and says he needs to learn whether he is “to have my reward in the end or not.”
evidence.supports: The declaration functions within sustained, purposeful courtship, giving slight support to relational undertaking force while remaining principally an avowal.

evidence.quotation_or_description: Brooke offers, “I’ll wait,” while Meg invokes her youth and her father’s view that it is too soon.
evidence.supports: A future commitment is articulated elsewhere in the exchange, showing why the highlighted declaration has some performative context but does not itself bear the full commitment.

ontology_assessment.diagnosis: T/P/E adequately represents the core utterance: it is overwhelmingly an avowal, with slight courtship-related undertaking force and no independently evidenced expressive/reflexive discharge.
